DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
# Review: Weekend Rate Restructure Proposal

The direction may well be right. Being £20–35 below a competitive set charging £165–180 suggests some headroom. But the three things you're most confident about don't hold up: the price-sensitivity test, the "conservative floor" revenue figure, and the low-risk framing of the two-night minimum. I'd revise before this goes to the GM.

## Major issues

### 1. The June→July "test" doesn't measure price sensitivity
This is the centrepiece of the case, and your own Table 1 undermines it.

- **The rise is fully explained by seasonality.** Section 2 says July and August are your strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. Occupancy climbs to 89% in July and 93% in August whatever the rate. A June-to-July comparison cannot separate the £10 rise from the summer peak.
- **There's no control.** To learn anything you'd need July 2025 against July 2024 (and ideally against competitor occupancy), or a comparison of booking pace before and after the change for the same arrival dates.
- **The timing is muddy.** The change was made in the last week of June, so July stays were partly booked at the old rate.
- **"The higher rate reinforced our positioning"** has no supporting evidence and should come out.

The honest conclusion is that you don't yet know your weekend price elasticity. The case can still be made, but it has to rest on competitor positioning and pick-up data, not on this test.

### 2. Room count: 112 or 124?
Section 2 says 112 rooms. The revenue calculation uses 124.

- 124 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ **£204k**
- 112 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ **£184k**

The headline is overstated by about £20k before any other adjustment. A reviewer will spot this, and it will damage confidence in the rest of the paper.

### 3. £204k is a ceiling, not a floor
The calculation applies £20 to every occupied weekend room. But the proposal only raises BAR, and it explicitly protects:
- corporate contracted rates,
- contracted group rates, including wedding blocks, which you say are about 38% of Saturday room bookings.

Some other weekend rooms will also sell at discounted, package or member rates, and OTA bookings incur commission on the uplift. Only the BAR-sold share of rooms gets the full £20. You need that mix from the PMS. The realistic uplift could plausibly be well under half the headline.

The calculation also assumes occupancy holds, which Section 3 can no longer support. So it is not "prudent" either.

### 4. The two-night minimum conflicts with your biggest Saturday segment
Section 4 describes wedding guests as about 38% of Saturday bookings, typically arriving Saturday and leaving Sunday. That is exactly the one-night Saturday stay the minimum prohibits. The proposal doesn't say how this is handled:

- If future wedding blocks are exempt, a large share of Saturday demand is outside the policy, and the "smoothing" benefit shrinks accordingly.
- If they're not exempt, you risk losing that business to competitors. You also risk your relationship with Quayside Hall, which is arguably a strategic asset worth more than the rate uplift.

There are further gaps:
- **There is no downside case.** A minimum turns away one-night Saturday guests who won't add a Friday or Sunday. You sold out on 31 Saturdays. On the other ~21, the restriction displaces demand rather than converting it.
- **It applies year-round.** In January (62%) and February (66%), turning away any Saturday booking is hard to justify. Minimum-stay rules are normally applied only on high-demand dates.
- **Competitors probably don't impose one.** Raising the price to match them and adding a restriction they don't have makes you less competitive, not equal.

Saying the minimum adds unquantified "material" upside, while ignoring its downside, is not conservative.

## Moderate issues

- **The value-for-money score is circular.** Guests rate you 8.4, the highest in your set, at least partly because you're the cheapest. Raising the price will likely lower it. That makes it evidence of headroom, not evidence of insensitivity.
- **The monitoring trigger is reasonable but untied to economics.** At £145→£165, room revenue breaks even if occupancy falls to about 87.9% of its previous level, roughly 79% → 69%, a drop of about 10 points. A 5-point trigger is therefore cautious on room revenue. Show this calculation, because it strengthens your case. However:
  - Lost guests also mean lost F&B and ancillary spend.
  - Reviewing monthly against 2025 means problems surface late. Weekend leisure books weeks ahead, so a weak month is largely locked in before you see it.
  - Launching on 1 June means the first readings come during peak season, which will mask any sensitivity. That is the same confound as in Section 3.
  - Weekly pick-up pace against 2025 for future dates would be a faster and better trigger.
- **The summer 2026 uplift is partly already lost.** Weekend stays from June to September already booked at £145 won't reprice, which affects year-one revenue.
- **"Recovered strongly since 2023"** is asserted without data.

## What's sound
- The competitor positioning is clear and internally consistent. At £165 you'd sit at the bottom of the set's range, not above it.
- Protecting existing corporate and group contracts is right.
- Having a defined review trigger at all is good practice.

## Suggested revisions
1. Replace the June→July test with July 2025 vs July 2024 and booking-pace data, or drop the claim and rest the case on competitive positioning.
2. Fix the room count and recompute using the actual BAR share of weekend room nights, net of OTA commission.
3. Present a range (downside, base, upside) with the breakeven occupancy shown, instead of a single "floor".
4. Either exempt wedding guests and apply the minimum only to high-demand Saturdays, or drop the minimum from this proposal and trial it separately.
5. Switch monitoring to weekly forward pick-up, with a defined response such as rolling back to £155 if pace drops below a set threshold.
6. Soften the recommendation wording. "The evidence shows our guests are not price sensitive" and "delivering at least £204,000" both overclaim.

Made with these changes, it becomes a credible, genuinely lower-risk proposal. As written, a sceptical GM or finance director could pick apart its main claims quickly.
